title: Everything Is Bound to Pass Away
intro: In accounts of the Basus War, Bujayr’s death brings al-Harith ibn Ubbad into a feud between Bakr and Taghlib that he had refused to join. Al-Asma'i transmits only a short set of verses, while later literary tradition gives the poem a much longer life. Al-Nahari recites thirty-seven verses from that long recension, beginning with the passing of earthly things and the worth of good deeds. Each call to bring up the mare al-Na'ama returns the listener to a different aspect of Bujayr’s loss.

translation: Everything is bound to pass away,
except my Lord and righteous deeds.
1.sharh: The opening of the longer recension sets transience against divine permanence and the lasting worth of good deeds. Soon the loss that prompts this reflection will have a name.

translation: You see the people all looking on.
None of them has any means around it.
2.sharh: Everyone is a witness to mortality. Being able to see it coming gives the onlookers no power to turn it aside.

translation: Tell Umm al-Agharr to weep for Bujayr.
Men have been parted from their wealth.
3.sharh: The speaker asks another person to carry the grief into the household. A dead man’s possessions survive him and are precisely what he can no longer reach.

translation: By my life, I shall weep for Bujayr
as long as water comes down from the mountain tops.
4.sharh: Runoff will come down the mountains with each new rain. That recurring movement supplies a measure for mourning that can have no appointed end.

translation: How I miss Bujayr when
the horses wheel on a day of desperate fighting,
5.sharh: The cry breaks off into a battlefield scene. This is an occasion on which Bujayr’s presence would have counted, and the next two verses keep developing it.

translation: when the armoured men pass deadly poison round
and the fair women emerge from their curtained rooms,
6.sharh: The warriors’ blows become a drink they serve one another. The danger has reached the tents too, bringing women out from the privacy of their curtained quarters.

translation: when every noble-faced woman runs, calling,
“Bakr, to our aid!” bright as a carved figure.
7.sharh: The tribal name is a cry for help. The speaker catches the woman in motion and at the same time gives her the sharply visible beauty of a carved figure.

translation: Bujayr, man of good deeds, no peace until
the wastes are filled with the heads of men,
8.sharh: He addresses the dead man as if he could hear an undertaking on his behalf. The image of the filled desert marks the point at which mourning turns into a vow of vengeance.

translation: and eyes grow cool again after weeping,
when blood gives drink to the spearheads.
9.sharh: Cool eyes are the Arabic image for relief. The terrible bargain in this line exchanges the flow of tears for another liquid that makes spearpoints seem to drink.

translation: Wa'il cries out under the war
like camels bawling under their loads.
10.sharh: Wa'il includes both sets of kin in the feud. Their collective outcry is given the familiar sound of an overloaded camel.

translation: God knows I was never among those who brought it on.
Today I am in the heat of its fire.
11.sharh: The speaker distinguishes the people who set the war going from the people its heat reaches. The change from past to present is his own entry into it.

translation: I kept out of Wa'il’s way so they might come to their senses.
Taghlib would not let me stand apart.
12.sharh: His absence had once expressed a hope for his kinsmen’s recovery of judgement. He now lays the loss of that freedom at Taghlib’s door.

translation: They turned my forelock grey over Bujayr.
They killed him unjustly, without a fight.
13.sharh: Grief becomes visible in a lock of grey hair. Bujayr died without the give and take of combat that might have made such a death intelligible to his father.

translation: They killed him for the strap of Kulayb’s sandal.
A noble life is dear at the price of a strap.
14.sharh: In the traditional account al-Muhalhil priced Bujayr’s life at a single thong from the dead Kulayb’s sandal. It is the deliberate smallness of the price that wounds.

translation: Children of Taghlib, be on your guard.
We have drunk from a cup of death, clear and sweet.
15.sharh: The cup is offered as an explanation for the warning. Those who can drink death like clear water have ceased to be deterred by their own danger.

translation: Children of Taghlib, you have killed a man
whose like we have never heard of in ages past.
16.sharh: The insult of the sandal strap receives a second answer. Set Bujayr against all remembered men, the father says, and he still has no equal.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
Wa'il’s war has conceived after standing barren.
17.sharh: Calling for the mare announces his decision to ride. In the next breath the war itself is pictured as a female that has conceived after a barren interval.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
What is wanted is my deed, beyond my words.
18.sharh: His own recurrent command is speech. Its purpose is to set something moving, to have the horse brought within reach.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
The women’s mourning has risen into loud lament.
19.sharh: The women’s voices give the command a setting. Each time he speaks, mourning can still be heard around him.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
My hair is grey. Women who spurn me do not know me.
20.sharh: The grey hair returns as a sign of an altered face. Women who already looked away from him can scarcely recognise the person grief has made.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me
for riding by night, at daybreak and in the evenings.
21.sharh: Three customary times of travel pass across the line. The horse is wanted for a commitment that extends round the clock.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
My night outlasts even the long nights.
22.sharh: Time has slowed for the father left awake. The recurring order supplies movement in a line otherwise given over to a night that will not end.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me
for champions to grapple with champions.
23.sharh: The word for an embrace makes opposing champions come bodily close. The same name for the fighters on either side heightens the symmetry.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
Turn aside, both of you, from foolish counsel.
24.sharh: The command is addressed to two people in Arabic. A second command gives the pair a choice of whom to listen to while fetching the mare.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
My heart will not forget the fight.
25.sharh: Delay might have cooled the wish to fight. The father claims his heart has remained fast on its purpose.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me
whenever the north wind trails past.
26.sharh: The wind acquires a trailing hem. A natural event that will keep recurring becomes the cue to ask for the mare again.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me
for Bujayr, who undid the prisoners’ fetters.
27.sharh: The father fixes on a service Bujayr once rendered to others. The man for whom he wants to ride is remembered here in the act of setting prisoners free.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me
for a generous man crowned with beauty.
28.sharh: Beauty becomes the son’s crown. It gives him in his father’s memory the place of honour denied him by the price set on his life.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me.
We do not sell men as sandals are sold.
29.sharh: The language of a market sale brings back Kulayb’s sandal. A comparison intended as an insult has become the father’s argument for refusing its terms.

translation: Bring al-Na'ama’s tether close to me
for Bujayr. My father’s brother and my mother’s brother be his ransom.
30.sharh: The two different Arabic words for uncle draw in both sides of the family. The conventional wish to ransom someone gives the father a way to say how dearly he values his son.

translation: Bring her for the clan of Taghlib, proud and fierce,
to grapple with armoured men on the day of fighting.
31.sharh: The mare is familiar enough for him simply to say “her”. The tribal name now resolves into the proud, armoured men he expects to encounter.

translation: Bring her, and bring my armour too,
smooth mail that turns the points of arrows.
32.sharh: The second half unfolds what he means by his gear. A smooth surface of metal links is set against the sharp points coming towards it.

translation: Bring her with blades honed thin and sharp
for the champions’ clash on the day they meet.
33.sharh: The thin edges complete the portrait of horse and rider. In the word for clashing, the imagined meeting of champions also has a sound.

translation: Many an army I have faced as it rained death,
on a tall horse lightly covered.
34.sharh: The tense turns back to what he claims to have done already. Against a whole army imagined as a rainstorm he sets the outline of a single mounted man.

translation: Ask noble Kinda and Bakr about us.
Ask Madhhij and the people of Hilal,
35.sharh: A string of tribal names gives the boast potential witnesses. The next verse recalls the occasion on which their testimony is supposed to rest.

translation: when they came against us with a great host,
grim in its menace and fierce in its onset.
36.sharh: Size first, then expression, then force of onset. The army gathers the features of a single threatening visitor whom the speaker must receive.

translation: When that army sought our hospitality, we served it
every keen-pointed, burnished blade.
37.sharh: Host and guest ordinarily meet over food. The two closely related words for hospitality set up that expectation before the last half delivers the bitter figure of the swords.

1.1.3.head: مَصير
1.1.3.meaning: The end to which something comes.

1.2.3-4.head: صالِح الأَعمال
1.2.3-4.meaning: “The good of deeds”, righteous acts considered in terms of their lasting worth.

2.2.5.head: اِحتِيال
2.2.5.meaning: Finding a stratagem or means of escape.

3.1.2-3.head: أُمّ الأَغَرّ
3.1.2-3.meaning: Umm al-Agharr, identified by Abu Hilal as al-Harith’s wife and called upon to mourn Bujayr.

3.1.5.head: بُجَير
3.1.5.meaning: Bujayr, killed by al-Muhalhil in the Basus tradition and usually identified as the speaker’s son.

3.2.1-2.head: حالَ بَينَ
3.2.1-2.meaning: “A barrier was put between”, cutting people off from something they held.

5.1.1-2.head: لَهف نَفسي
5.1.1-2.meaning: “The anguish of my soul”, a cry for someone dearly missed.

5.2.5.head: عُضال
5.2.5.meaning: Grievous and hard to overcome, also said of an intractable illness.

6.2.2.head: البيض
6.2.2.meaning: Fair women, identified here by the curtained quarters from which they emerge.

6.2.4-5.head: قِباب الحِجال
6.2.4-5.meaning: “The domes of the curtained chambers”, women’s private, tented quarters.

7.2.1-2.head: يا لَبَكر
7.2.1-2.meaning: “Bakr, come to our aid.” The prefixed Arabic particle marks the people being called to the rescue.

7.2.3.head: غَرّاء
7.2.3.meaning: Bright-faced and striking to look at.

8.2.1.head: مَلَأَ
8.2.1.meaning: The wastes are to be filled. The diwan has “we fill”, naming the speaker and his people as the agents.

8.2.2.head: البيد
8.2.2.meaning: The open desert wastes. Filling so vast a space measures the scale of the vengeance he vows.

9.1.1-2.head: قَرَّتِ العَين
9.1.1-2.meaning: “The eyes grow cool”, grief giving way to relief.

9.2.5.meaning: The upper shafts of spears, close to the heads.

10.1.2.head: وائِل
10.1.2.meaning: Wa'il, the common ancestor whose name includes the two sides, Bakr and Taghlib.

10.1.3.head: عَجَّ
10.1.3.meaning: To cry out loudly under pain or a load.

11.1.4.head: جُناة
11.1.4.meaning: Those responsible for bringing a war about.

11.2.4.head: صالٍ
11.2.4.meaning: One exposed to a fire’s heat.

12.1.5.head: أَفاقَ
12.1.5.meaning: To recover one’s senses, here to come round to more reasonable conduct.

12.2.2.head: تَغلِب
12.2.2.meaning: Taghlib, the branch of Wa'il opposing Bakr in the Basus narratives.

14.1.2-4.head: شِسع نَعل كُلَيب
14.1.2-4.meaning: “For Kulayb’s sandal strap”. In the feud story al-Muhalhil claims that Bujayr’s death pays for the thong alone.

15.2.5.head: زُلال
15.2.5.meaning: Clear, sweet and easy to swallow.

16.2.5.meaning: The ages that have gone before.

17.1.2-3.head: مَربِط النَّعامَة
17.1.2-3.meaning: Al-Na'ama is the mare’s name. Calling for her tether or tethering place is a way of calling for the horse.

17.2.1.head: لَقِحَ
17.2.1.meaning: To conceive, said of war as if it could bear offspring.

17.2.5.head: حِيال
17.2.5.meaning: A season without conceiving, of a female animal.

20.2.4.meaning: Women who spurn him, the reading Cheikho prints. Abu Hilal reads “the perfumes no longer knew it”, explaining that he gave up perfume after his son’s death.

21.2.3.head: الآصال
21.2.3.meaning: The hours of late afternoon and evening.

22.2.3-5.head: عَلى اللَّيالي الطِّوال
22.2.3-5.meaning: “Beyond the long nights”, longer even than nights already felt to drag.

23.2.1.head: اِعتِناق
23.2.1.meaning: An embrace, transferred here to champions grappling at close quarters.

24.2.1-2.head: اِعدِلا عَن
24.2.1-2.meaning: “You two, turn aside from”, a dual command to disregard the suggestion.

25.2.5.head: سالٍ
25.2.5.meaning: One who has forgotten or ceased to care.

26.2.4-5.head: ذَيل الشَّمال
26.2.4-5.meaning: “The hem of the north wind”, its trailing sweep along the ground.

27.2.2-3.head: مُفَكِّك الأَغلال
27.2.2-3.meaning: “The loosener of fetters”, one who sets captives free.

28.2.2.head: مُتَوَّج
28.2.2.meaning: Crowned, with beauty imagined as a visible diadem.

29.2.4-5.head: بَيع النِّعال
29.2.4-5.meaning: “The sale of sandals”, an allusion to the price named for Bujayr’s life.

30.2.2.head: فَدى
30.2.2.meaning: To give someone as a ransom. Here the wish conveys how dearly the dead man is held.

31.1.4.head: شوس
31.1.4.meaning: Proud and fierce, literally looking at someone out of the corner of the eye.

32.1.3.head: لَأمَة
32.1.3.meaning: A warrior’s equipment, specified here as body armour.

32.2.2.head: دِلاص
32.2.2.meaning: Smooth, describing the surface of finely made mail.

33.1.2.head: مُرهَفات
33.1.2.meaning: Blades ground to a thin cutting edge.

33.2.1.head: قِراع
33.2.1.meaning: An exchange of blows, with the suggestion of their ringing sound.

34.2.4.head: الجِلال
34.2.4.meaning: Horsecloths laid across the animal’s back.

35.1.2.head: كِندَة
35.1.2.meaning: Kinda, a tribal people known for their rulers and alliances in Arabia.

35.2.2.head: مَذحِج
35.2.2.meaning: Madhhij, the collective name of a group of southern Arabian tribes.

35.2.3-4.head: حَيّ هِلال
35.2.3-4.meaning: The people of Hilal, named among the tribal witnesses to the speaker’s deeds.

36.1.5.head: زُهاء
36.1.5.meaning: Great numbers or the imposing appearance of a large force.

36.2.1.head: مُكفَهِرّ
36.2.1.meaning: Scowling or forbidding, giving the host the features of a face.

36.2.4.head: المَصال
36.2.4.meaning: The force of an onset or charge.

37.1.4.head: قِرى
37.1.4.meaning: The fare offered to a guest, used ironically for what meets the oncoming force.

37.2.3.head: الذُّباب
37.2.3.meaning: The point or cutting extremity of a sword.
